lead: Gauss's law: net electric flux through a closed surface depends only on charge inside. Outside charges add field but no net flux. It works because a point charge's field falls as 1/r², matching a sphere's area growth r², so flux is same at every radius. Engineers use it to get fields of lines, sheets, cables, spheres and conductors in one step.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for surface integrals and the divergence theorem, and Chapter 3.2 for a point charge's field.

sections.h3: Flux, and the two forms of Gauss's law

blocks.text: Electric flux counts field lines crossing a surface. For a closed surface, Φ = ∮ E·dS. E is field in N/C at a small patch, dS is that patch's outward area in m², and the dot product keeps only the perpendicular part. Flux is in N·m²/C.

blocks.where: Φ is net outward flux in N·m²/C; E is field in N/C; dS is outward area element in m²; Q_enclosed is net charge inside in C; ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²) is permittivity of free space.

blocks.text: Net flux out of any closed surface equals enclosed charge divided by ε₀. The surface is imaginary. Outside charges give field at the surface, but their lines enter and leave, so they add no net Φ.
The divergence theorem from Chapter 3.1 gives the differential form.

blocks.where: ∇·E is divergence of E in (N/C)/m; ρ is volume charge density in C/m³; ε₀ is as above.

blocks.text: Both forms say charge is the source of field lines. This is one of Maxwell's equations and returns in Chapter 3.8.

sections.h3: Line charge and sheet: pick the surface

items: Spot the symmetry: flat, cylindrical or spherical.
Draw a closed surface where E is constant and perpendicular, or parallel to the surface.
Write Φ face by face: E times area, or zero.
Get Q_enclosed from the charge density.
Divide by ε₀ and solve for E.

blocks.text: Infinite line charge, density λ C/m. Take a coaxial cylinder of radius r and length L. On the curved wall E is radial and constant, so flux is E × 2πrL; on the flat caps E lies along the surface, so flux is zero. Enclosed charge is λL.

blocks.where: λ is charge per unit length in C/m; r is perpendicular distance from the line in m; E points radially away from a positive line.

blocks.text: Infinite sheet, surface charge density σ C/m². Take a pillbox of face area A crossing the sheet. Each face carries flux EA and sides carry none, so 2EA = σA/ε₀.

blocks.where: σ is charge per unit area in C/m²; E is uniform, perpendicular to the sheet, points away from positive charge on both sides, and does not depend on distance.

blocks.text: Thin shell of radius R carrying total charge Q. For r > R the Gaussian sphere encloses all Q, so the shell behaves like a point charge at its centre: E = kQ/r². For r < R it encloses no charge, so E = 0 inside.
E = Q / (4π ε₀ r²) = kQ / r²   (r > R);   E = 0   (r < R)
blocks.where: Q is total charge in C; r is distance from centre in m; R is shell radius in m; k = 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².

blocks.text: Solid sphere of radius R with Q uniform, so ρ = Q/((4/3)πR³). At radius r < R the Gaussian sphere encloses only Q r³/R³, so flux grows as r³ while area grows as r².
E = kQ r / R³ inside (r < R);   E = kQ / r² outside (r > R)
blocks.where: r is distance from centre in m; R is sphere radius in m; inside field points radially outward and is zero only at the centre.

blocks.text: Inside, E climbs linearly from zero to kQ/R² at the surface; outside it falls as 1/r². A shell and a solid ball with same Q and R have identical fields outside.

sections.h3: Conductors, and why the law matters

blocks.text: In electrostatic equilibrium the field inside a conductor is zero, else free electrons would drift. Any closed surface wholly inside the metal has zero flux, so encloses zero charge. All excess charge sits on the outer surface. A charge inside a cavity induces opposite charge on the inner wall, but outside sees only the outer surface — a hollow conductor shields its cavity from outside fields.
Just outside a conductor, take a pillbox with one face inside the metal (E = 0) and one just outside. Only the outer face carries flux, so EA = σA/ε₀.
E = σ / ε₀  (just outside a conductor)
blocks.where: σ is local surface charge density in C/m²; E is normal to the surface and points away from positive charge.

blocks.text: Charge collects where curvature is sharp, so σ and E are large at points. Air breaks down near 3 × 10⁶ V/m. Lightning rods are pointed so the high tip field ionises air and starts discharge. High-voltage busbars and corona rings are rounded so σ and E stay below breakdown. Gauss's law also gives the D-field form used in Chapter 3.5.

figure.caption: The outer box is all charge in space; only q₁ and q₂ inside the inner box fix net flux through the closed surface. Outside charges change field on the surface, not flux.

spec.aria: The outer box holds every charge in space; only charges inside the inner box fix net flux through the closed surface.

examples.question: An infinite line carries uniform charge density λ = 5 μC/m. Using a cylindrical Gaussian surface, find E at r = 10 cm from the line. Take ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻².
steps: Symmetry: E is radial and equal on a coaxial cylinder.
Gaussian surface: cylinder of radius r = 0.10 m and length L, coaxial with the line.
Curved wall: dS is parallel to E, so flux is E × 2πrL.
Flat caps: dS is perpendicular to E, so flux is 0 each.
Enclosed charge: Q_enclosed = λL = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × L coulomb.
Gauss's law: E × 2πrL = λL/ε₀. L cancels, giving E = λ/(2πε₀r).
Direction: radially away from the line, since λ is positive.
examples.answer: E = 8.99 × 10⁵ N/C, pointing radially away from the line.
examples.check:
import math
lam = 5e-6
eps0 = 8.854e-12
r = 0.10
E = lam/(2*math.pi*eps0*r)
print(round(E/1e5, 2))

traps: Putting a charge outside the surface into Q_enclosed. It adds to E everywhere but gives zero net flux — zero flux never means zero field.
Using E = σ/ε₀ for a free thin sheet. A free sheet gives σ/2ε₀; σ/ε₀ belongs to a conductor surface, where field exists on one side only.
Losing the sign of Φ by dropping outward dS. Negative Q_enclosed means net inward flux.
Assuming E = 0 inside a uniformly charged solid sphere because it is zero inside a shell. Inside the ball E = kQr/R³, rising from zero at the centre.
Treating the shell as continuous at r = R. Just inside E is zero and just outside it is kQ/R²; the jump exists because the shell is taken as infinitely thin.

quiz.q: State Gauss's law in integral form and name each symbol with its unit.
quiz.a: ∮E·dS = Q_enclosed/ε₀. E is field in N/C, dS is outward area element in m², Φ is net outward flux in N·m²/C, Q_enclosed is net enclosed charge in C, ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²).

quiz.q: A point charge sits outside a closed surface. Is flux through the surface zero? Is field on the surface zero?
quiz.a: Flux is zero: every line that enters also leaves. Field is not zero — the outside charge contributes to E at every surface point. Gauss's law constrains only net flux, not E.

quiz.q: An infinite sheet carries σ = 2 μC/m². Find field at 5 cm and how it changes at 50 cm.
quiz.a: E = σ/(2ε₀) = (2 × 10⁻⁶)/(2 × 8.854 × 10⁻¹²) = 1.13 × 10⁵ N/C. For an infinite sheet E does not depend on distance, so at 50 cm it is the same, 1.13 × 10⁵ N/C, normal to the sheet.

quiz.q: A thin spherical shell of radius 0.2 m carries 4 μC. Find E at 0.1 m and 0.4 m from the centre.
quiz.a: At r = 0.1 m < R the Gaussian sphere encloses no charge, so E = 0. At r = 0.4 m, E = kQ/r² = (9 × 10⁹)(4 × 10⁻⁶)/(0.4)² = 2.25 × 10⁵ N/C, radially outward.

quiz.q: Why must excess charge on a conductor in equilibrium lie on its outer surface?
quiz.a: Field inside a conductor at rest is zero, else charges would move. Any closed surface wholly inside the metal then has zero flux, so encloses zero charge. Charge can sit only on the boundary.

quiz.q: A solid sphere of radius R carries charge Q uniformly. Compare field at r = R/2 with field at r = 2R.
quiz.a: Inside, E = kQr/R³, so at R/2, E = kQ/(2R²). Outside, E = kQ/r², so at 2R, E = kQ/(4R²). Ratio is 2 : 1 — twice as strong at R/2. Both point radially outward.

quiz.q: A cube sits in uniform field E along x-axis. What is net flux? What if charge q is at its centre?
quiz.a: Uniform field: zero net flux, since lines entering one face leave the opposite face and Q_enclosed = 0. With q at centre, net flux becomes q/ε₀, shared equally by six faces — each face gets q/(6ε₀).

quiz.q: What does ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ say at a point, and what is it in a charge-free region?
quiz.a: Divergence of E at a point equals local charge density there divided by ε₀ — a measure of how strongly field lines start there. In a charge-free region ρ = 0, so ∇·E = 0 and field lines pass through without starting or ending.

beyond: Not for the exam. Field solvers for antennas, PCBs and MEMS solve ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ on a mesh rather than summing Coulomb's law point by point. Replace charge by mass and the same law gives Gauss's law for gravity, used to model planetary interiors. High-voltage engineers shape corona rings and busbar ends so local σ stays under air's breakdown value. Search next: finite element electrostatics, corona discharge, Gauss's law for gravity.
